stem: Patient says: "The floor seems to swim when I walk in my first progressives." Remarking shows the fitting crosses centered on her pupils and the PDs are correct, but the frame sits nearly vertical with almost no face form. What is the best next step?
choices: Remake the lenses on a steeper base curve
Adjust the frame for more pantoscopic tilt and face form
Increase the add power by +0.50 D
Remake the lenses in a design with a longer corridor
explanation: Once PD and fitting height are confirmed, IOT's troubleshooting table lists too little pantoscopic tilt and too little facial wrap as causes of a swimming sensation, with frame adjustment as the remedy. A longer corridor, a stronger add or a base-curve change does nothing for a position-of-wear problem; adjust first and remake only if that fails.

source.title: IOT: Troubleshooting Progressive Lenses

stem: Patient says: "I have to tip my head way back to read with my new progressives." Add power, monocular PDs and fitting heights all verify, but the new design has a noticeably longer corridor than her previous pair. What is the most likely fix?
choices: Lower both fitting heights 2 mm so the near zone sits lower
Remake in a design with a shorter corridor
Reduce the add 0.25 D so she can read from farther away
Increase the vertex distance so the near zone widens
explanation: A corridor that is too long places full add power low in the lens, so the wearer raises her chin to drop her eyes far enough to reach it. IOT lists this as a cause of tilting the head up to read, with a shorter corridor as the remedy. Lowering the heights or reducing tilt would push the near zone even further out of reach.

source.title: IOT: Troubleshooting Progressive Lenses

topic: Case: PAL fitting height too high
stem: Patient says: "I have to drop my chin to see the TV clearly in my new progressives." When you remark the lenses, the fitting crosses sit about 3 mm above her pupil centers. What is the most likely cause and fix?
choices: Fitting height too low; raise the frame on the face
Add too weak; increase the add power
Monocular PDs reversed; swap the lenses
Fitting height too high; lower the frame or remake lower
explanation: With the fitting crosses above the pupils, her straight-ahead gaze falls into the top of the corridor where plus power is already building, so distance blurs and she tucks her chin to look higher in the lens. IOT attributes tilting the head forward for distance to a segment height that is too high and recommends adjusting the frame or remaking.

source.title: IOT: Troubleshooting Progressive Lenses

topic: Case: PAL fitting height too low
stem: Patient says reading is blurry and the reading area is hard to find in her new progressives. Remarked fitting crosses sit about 2 mm below her pupil centers; the rest of the adjustment is good. What is the best response?
choices: Raise the fitting crosses by adjustment, or remake at the correct height
Increase the vertex distance to widen the near zone
Remake with a wider PD so the near zones line up
Leave the heights and increase the add +0.50 D so the lower lens reads clearly
explanation: When the fitting cross sits below the pupil, the entire progression moves down and the near zone ends up near the bottom of the lens. IOT lists a segment height that is too low as a cause of blurry near vision; 20/20's Problem Solving 101 notes the fitting cross can be raised or lowered with nose-pad adjustment, otherwise reorder with correct heights.

source.title: IOT: Troubleshooting Progressive Lenses

stem: Patient says she has to turn her head slightly to get her new progressives clear at intermediate and near. Measured monocular PDs were R 30.5 / L 33.5 mm, but the lab made both lenses at 32.0 mm. What is the problem?
choices: Add face form so the corridors swing into line with her eyes
Accept: the total PD of 64 mm is correct, so the pair is within tolerance
Each cross is 1.5 mm off, outside the ±1.0 mm PAL tolerance; remake
The add is too strong and should be reduced before remaking
explanation: Progressive corridors are narrow, so they must be placed on each eye's monocular PD. ANSI Z80.1-2015 requires each PAL fitting cross to be within ±1.0 mm of the specified monocular PD; a correct total PD does not compensate for 1.5 mm errors per eye. Looking to the side to focus is the classic symptom of misplaced corridors.

source.title: The Vision Council: ANSI Z80.1-2015 Quick Reference Guide

topic: Case: PAL in a shallow frame
stem: A patient picked a narrow frame; her measured progressive fitting height was 14 mm. Two weeks later she says the reading area is tiny and she has to look almost to the bottom edge of the lens. What should have been done when ordering?
choices: Order the fitting height 2 mm lower than measured
Specify a flatter base curve
Order a lower add power
Recommend a short-corridor design or a deeper frame
explanation: 20/20's remake-prevention lesson advises recommending a short fit (or a deeper frame) whenever the measured height is under about 16 mm; otherwise the near and intermediate zones are cut off or squeezed into the bottom of the lens. Lowering the height would make it worse, and add or base curve doesn't create vertical room.

source.title: 20/20 Magazine CE: Tips to Decrease Remakes, Part 2

topic: Case: Same PAL design, new Rx
stem: Patient says: "My last progressives were fine, these are awful." The office reordered the same design and corridor; only the Rx changed, with the add rising from +1.75 to +2.50. Measurements and adjustment verify. What does progressive troubleshooting guidance point to?
choices: The new Rx changes how the design performs; reconsider progression length
Raise the fitting height 2 mm and reorder the same design and corridor
Match the old pair's base curve; the add change doesn't matter
A lab error, because an identical design must perform identically for any Rx
explanation: IOT notes that when the same design is repeat-dispensed after a prescription change, the design's behavior can change dramatically, and the usual culprit is progression length. Treat every PAL wearer like a new fit: re-evaluate design and corridor for the new Rx rather than assuming the old choice still works.

source.title: IOT: Troubleshooting Progressive Lenses

topic: Case: PAL wearer reading off to the side
stem: A progressive wearer sees well at distance and intermediate, but says she must hold reading material far to the left to see it clearly. The frame is properly adjusted and the fitting crosses align with her pupils. What is the best next step?
choices: Switch to a longer-corridor design so the near zone is wider
Find her true near points with the mirror-dot technique and order from those
Lower both fitting heights by 2 mm so the near zone sits closer to her gaze
Increase the add by +0.50 D so she can read through the edge of the near zone
explanation: Optometry Times describes this case: the patient isn't converging down and in through the near circles. Placing a dotted flat mirror at her working distance and marking where her lines of sight cross the lenses gives her true near PD, which the lab can use to position the near zones. The add and heights are not the problem.

source.title: Optometry Times: Troubleshooting optical complaints

topic: Case: Induced prism from wide OCs
stem: A -6.00 D OU single-vision wearer says her new glasses "pull" and tire her eyes. Her PD is 62 mm, but the lensmeter shows the optical centers 68 mm apart. What is the induced prism?
choices: About 1.8Δ base-in total, within tolerance
About 3.6Δ base-in total, outside tolerance; remake
None, because a decentered minus lens induces no prism
About 3.6Δ base-out total, outside tolerance; remake
explanation: Prentice's rule (prism = power × decentration in cm): each eye looks 3 mm nasal to its OC, so 6.00 × 0.3 = 1.8Δ per lens. A minus lens has its base toward the edge, so a point nasal to the OC is base-in; the two lenses add to 3.6Δ BI. For powers over ±2.75 D, ANSI allows only 2.5 mm of PD error, so 6 mm fails.

source.title: 20/20 Magazine: Understanding the Prismatic Effect

topic: Case: Readers made at distance PD
stem: Patient picks up +2.50 single-vision readers and says they pull her eyes when she reads. Her PD is 64/61 mm, and the lensmeter shows the optical centers 64 mm apart. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The OCs were set to her distance PD instead of her near PD
The add is too weak for her reading distance
The frame has too much pantoscopic tilt for reading
The base curve wasn't matched to her old readers, causing a pull
explanation: NAO's SOAP course lists a correctly measured PD that was ordered incorrectly (distance PD instead of near) as a cause of a pulling sensation. Reading glasses should be centered on the near PD; here each OC is 1.5 mm too far out, inducing base-in prism with plus lenses, which the eyes feel as strain.

source.title: NAO CE: Use SOAP to Solve Eyewear Problems, Part 2

stem: A patient's Rx changed by only -0.25 D, yet she says her new single-vision glasses feel pulled and "different." Her old lenses were on a 6.00 D base curve; the new spherical CR-39 lenses came back on a 4.00 D base. What is the best fix?
choices: Reduce the pantoscopic tilt
Add face form to the frame
Keep them; base curve affects only appearance
Remake on the same base curve as her previous pair
explanation: NAO's guidance: when the Rx change is less than 1 D, match the base curve of the previous eyewear; when the change exceeds 1 D, or the lens is aspheric or digitally designed, let the lab compute the best base curve. A 2 D base-curve jump changes magnification and peripheral optics enough to cause a pulling complaint.

source.title: NAO CE: Use SOAP to Solve Eyewear Problems, Part 2

topic: Case: OC height with pantoscopic tilt
stem: You are ordering single-vision lenses. With the frame adjusted to 10° of pantoscopic tilt, the patient's pupil centers are 24 mm above the lowest point of the lens shape. What OC height should you specify?
choices: 29 mm
22 mm
24 mm
19 mm
explanation: For every 2° of pantoscopic tilt, the optical center should be dropped 1 mm below the pupil so the optical axis passes through the eye's center of rotation. 10° of tilt means a 5 mm drop: 24 - 5 = 19 mm. Ignoring tilt (24 mm) is a classic cause of a pulling complaint.

source.title: 20/20 Magazine: The Well-Adjusted Frame

stem: A -2.00 D OU patient's prescription sunglasses in a steeply wrapped 8-base frame were made with standard, uncompensated lenses. He says they strain his eyes and the world looks "off." What is the best solution?
choices: Add base-out prism to each lens
Increase the pantoscopic tilt
Reorder as a wrap-compensated Rx with prism compensation
Reorder on a 4-base curve to match his dress glasses
explanation: Rotating a lens around a vertical axis (wrap) induces base-out prism and changes effective power. NAO recommends a wrap-compensated Rx and/or base-in prism to offset it. More base-out would make the problem worse, and a flat 4-base lens doesn't fit an 8-base frame.

source.title: NAO CE: Use SOAP to Solve Eyewear Problems, Part 2

stem: A patient refracted at -8.00 D with a 14 mm vertex distance chose a frame with no nose pads that sits at 10 mm. She says the new glasses seem too strong. What power should have been ordered for that frame position?
explanation: Moving a minus lens closer to the eye makes it effectively stronger. Using the approximation from 20/20's Problem Solving 101 (power² ÷ 1000 × mm of change): 64 ÷ 1000 × 4 ≈ 0.25 D, so the lens fit 4 mm closer should be ordered at -7.75 D. Adding minus would compound the overcorrection.

source.title: 20/20 Magazine CE: Problem Solving 101

stem: A +9.00 D wearer says his glasses suddenly seem too strong at distance. You notice the frame has slid down his nose so the lenses sit well farther from his eyes than at the fitting. What explains it?
choices: A plus lens moved away from the eye loses effective power, so it's under-correcting
A plus lens moved away from the eye gains effective plus power
Vertex distance matters only for minus lenses, so look for a lab error
The slipping frame is inducing base-out prism at distance
explanation: Plus lenses gain effective power as they move away from the eye and lose power as they move closer (the reverse of minus lenses). At +9.00 D, a few millimeters of extra vertex produces a noticeable overcorrection. Readjust the frame to the fitted vertex distance before considering any remake.

source.title: 20/20 Magazine CE: Problem Solving 101

stem: A 30-year-old receiving her first distance glasses (+1.50 OU) says, "Everything looks too strong; I see better without them." The lenses verify and fit well. What is the best response?
choices: Explain she's been accommodating, and allow 1-2 weeks to adapt
Add base-in prism to both lenses for comfort
Remake in a higher-index material to reduce magnification
Remake at +0.75 OU right away, since she prefers no correction
explanation: NAO notes that first-time hyperopes are used to accommodating to overcome their hyperopia, so a full correction can feel too strong at first. The recommended approach is education, reassurance and one to two weeks of adaptation before any change is considered; the optician shouldn't alter the prescription.

source.title: NAO CE: Use SOAP to Solve Eyewear Problems, Part 1

topic: Case: Blur at the sides after a frame change
stem: A patient moved from a frame with generous face form to a flat-fronted frame. She now sees blur, and the edge of the frame, when she looks to the sides. What is the best adjustment?
choices: Remake with a flatter base curve to reduce edge blur
Reduce the pantoscopic tilt
Increase vertex distance so the frame edge falls outside her view
Add face form to move the lens periphery out of her line of sight
explanation: Going from a wrapped to a flat frame moves the optically inferior periphery (marginal astigmatism) and the frame edge into the line of sight. 20/20's Problem Solving 101 recommends adding a bit of face form to move the lens edge back out of view; more vertex would actually widen the problem.

source.title: 20/20 Magazine CE: Problem Solving 101

topic: Case: Wavy floor in single vision
stem: A -3.00 D wearer says vision through her new glasses is clear straight ahead, but the floor looks wavy when she walks. The lenses verify. Which adjustment combination is recommended first?
choices: Increase vertex distance only
Decrease vertex, and increase pantoscopic tilt and face form
Increase vertex distance, reduce tilt and flatten face form
Remove all tilt so the lenses hang vertical
explanation: Optometry Times describes three adjustments that move peripheral aberrations out of the field of view: shorter vertex, more pantoscopic tilt and more face form. It notes the exceptions: prescriptions over ±7.00 D and unbalanced prescriptions (1.50 D or more difference), where tilt and wrap can create new problems.

source.title: Optometry Times: Troubleshooting optical complaints

stem: Patient in new polycarbonate lenses (-5.00 OU) says she sees color fringes, "rainbows," around bright objects when she looks off to the side. What is the most likely cause?
choices: Too much pantoscopic tilt in the frame
Chromatic aberration from the material's low Abbe value
Over-tightened eyewire screws stressing the lens
A missing UV-blocking treatment
explanation: Polycarbonate and many high-index plastics have low Abbe values, so white light disperses into colors, especially off-axis in stronger powers. 20/20's Problem Solving 101 advises fitting the lens as close to the eye as possible and adding face form; a higher-Abbe material is the other fix. An exposed polished edge can also cause internal rainbows.

source.title: 20/20 Magazine CE: Problem Solving 101

stem: Patient says that through her new glasses she feels shorter, as if walking uphill, with her surroundings looming tall. Which unwanted prism does this symptom point to?
choices: Base-in prism
Base-up prism
Base-out prism
Base-down prism
explanation: Light bends toward the base and the image shifts toward the apex. Base-down prism displaces images upward, producing the "inside a bowl, walking uphill" feeling; base-up gives a walking-downhill sensation. 20/20's Problem Solving 101 recommends marking the lens and checking for prism where the patient actually looks.

source.title: 20/20 Magazine CE: Problem Solving 101

stem: One lens of a progressive pair was remade after a scratch. The patient now reports eyestrain and slight vertical doubling. What should you check first?
choices: The base curve of the remade lens against the original lens
Prism at both PRPs, to confirm the thinning prism is equal
The add power of the original lens, in case it was also wrong
The pantoscopic tilt of the frame after the lens swap
explanation: Progressives are usually made with yoked base-down prism thinning, which is harmless only when it is equal in both eyes. 20/20's Problem Solving 101 warns that a single remade lens can carry a different amount; check both PRPs, apply the rules for canceling and compounding prism, and remake if they are uneven.

source.title: 20/20 Magazine CE: Problem Solving 101

topic: Case: Adapted to old centration error
stem: A patient wore his old glasses for years with optical centers well off his PD. His new, correctly centered lenses feel wrong to him. What approach does the guidance suggest?
choices: Duplicate the old centration error exactly, since he's adapted
Add base-in prism to both lenses to mimic the old pair's feel
Split the difference now, then go fully correct on the next pair
Order a lower-index material so the induced prism feels weaker
explanation: A patient can adapt to prism induced by long-standing centration errors. 20/20's Problem Solving 101 recommends a compromise: split the difference between correct centration and what he's used to, then bring him to zero induced prism on the next pair. Permanently copying a known error isn't good practice.

source.title: 20/20 Magazine CE: Problem Solving 101

topic: Case: Anisometrope reading through a bifocal
stem: A flat-top bifocal wearer (OD -1.00 DS, OS -4.00 DS) says words double vertically when she reads. The lenses verify. What is the standard solution?
choices: Reverse slab (molded base-down) on the left lens
Raise both segment heights 2 mm
Slab-off on the left lens
Slab-off (bicentric grind) on the right lens
explanation: Looking down through the segments of unequal lenses induces vertical imbalance; NAO flags differences over 1.5 D in the vertical meridian. Slab-off (bicentric grinding) adds base-up prism to the most minus or least plus lens, here the OS. Reverse slab is molded base-down prism on the most plus or least minus lens, which would be the OD.

source.title: NAO CE: Use SOAP to Solve Eyewear Problems, Part 2

stem: A patient with OD +3.00 DS and OS +1.00 DS reads through single-vision lenses at a point 10 mm below the optical centers. What vertical imbalance is induced?
choices: None, because both lenses are plus and the effects match
2.0Δ, right eye base-up relative to the left
4.0Δ, right eye base-up, since the prisms add together
2.0Δ, with the right eye base-down relative to the left
explanation: Prentice's rule: OD 3.00 × 1.0 = 3Δ and OS 1.00 × 1.0 = 1Δ. Below the OC of a plus lens the base is up, so both are base-up; prisms in the same direction cancel, leaving 2Δ net base-up OD. That exceeds the roughly 1.5Δ that 20/20 cites as the practical limit for comfortable fusion.

source.title: 20/20 Magazine: Understanding the Prismatic Effect

stem: Patient says her new glasses give her double vision, and it persists with one eye covered. The lenses and fit check out. What is the best action?
choices: Order slab-off on the weaker lens to balance the images
Refer to the doctor; this points to an ocular cause like cataract
Add vertical prism to the affected eye to fuse the two images
Remake with AR coating to remove the second image from reflections
explanation: Double vision that remains with one eye closed is monocular and can't be caused by binocular prism imbalance. NAO's course links monocular diplopia to ocular conditions such as cataract and directs the optician to the doctor's notes or a referral. Prism and slab-off address binocular problems only.

source.title: NAO CE: Use SOAP to Solve Eyewear Problems, Part 2

stem: An executive-bifocal wearer reports a faint ghost image when looking near the segment line. The prescription and segment heights verify. What can help?
choices: Polarized lenses to block light reflected off the ledge
A stronger add, since ghosting means the near power is weak
More vertex distance so the ledge sits farther from the eye
Anti-reflective coating to reduce scatter from the ledge
explanation: NAO notes that looking through the ledge of a bifocal or trifocal, especially an executive, can produce a doubling complaint, and AR coating can sometimes help because the symptom is aggravated by light scatter off the ledge. If adjustment doesn't resolve it, refer back to the doctor.

source.title: NAO CE: Use SOAP to Solve Eyewear Problems, Part 2

topic: Case: Distance not as sharp as expected
stem: Patient says distance vision in her new glasses isn't as sharp as she expected. Adjustment is correct and the lenses verify to the Rx. What is the next appropriate check?
choices: Over-refract the distance zone with ±0.25 D flippers
Order AR coating, since reflections reduce sharpness
Remake in a higher-index material for sharper optics
Add 2° of pantoscopic tilt and recheck in a week
explanation: NAO's SOAP method: recheck adjustment, re-verify, then use a trial-lens over-refraction, starting with +0.25 and -0.25 over the distance zone (or +0.25 OU over the reading area with a flipper). The result tells you whether a prescription question should go back to the doctor.

source.title: NAO CE: Use SOAP to Solve Eyewear Problems, Part 1

stem: A patient sees only 20/40 through glasses that verify and fit well, and a ±0.25 over-refraction doesn't help. What should the optician do?
choices: Change to a progressive design for a larger clear zone
Refer the patient back to the prescribing doctor
Recommend a polarized lens to boost contrast
Remake with 0.50 D more sphere to push acuity higher
explanation: When best-corrected acuity is below expectation and the eyewear checks out, NAO points to possible ocular causes, such as macular degeneration, cataract, corneal irregularity, dry eye, amblyopia or diabetes, and directs a referral to the doctor. The optician shouldn't keep changing lenses to chase a medical cause.

source.title: NAO CE: Use SOAP to Solve Eyewear Problems, Part 1

stem: A patient whose blood sugar was recently uncontrolled says that over three months she now reads better without glasses, but distance is blurrier. She wants new glasses today. What is the best counsel?
choices: Explain it may keep shifting until her sugar stabilizes; involve the doctor
Recommend polarized lenses, since the blur comes from glare
Order today's prescription now; refractive changes from blood sugar are permanent
Increase her add so near and distance balance out again
explanation: Eyes On Eyecare describes this case: unstable glucose causes refractive shifts that continue as sugars stabilize. The recommendation is to encourage blood sugar control and wait before finalizing, using an interim option or a lab redo policy if she needs glasses now.

source.title: Eyes On Eyecare: Top 5 Tips for Troubleshooting New Glasses Complaints

stem: Sphere and cylinder powers match the patient's old pair, but the cylinder axis changed by 20°. She says straight lines look tilted and she feels "off." The lenses verify to the Rx. What is the best next step?
choices: Add base-down prism
Remake at the old axis without contacting the prescriber
Consult the prescriber about an axis closer to the old one
Add face form to the frame
explanation: A large axis change can tilt and distort lines and cause an "off" feeling even when it is optically correct. Eyes On Eyecare suggests the prescriber check both eyes open and, if needed, shift the axis toward the old one by no more than 5-10° at a time. Changing the Rx is the prescriber's call, not the optician's.

source.title: Eyes On Eyecare: Top 5 Tips for Troubleshooting New Glasses Complaints

stem: Patient says she has to hold everything closer than she likes to see clearly with her new reading glasses. The lenses verify to the Rx. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The add is too weak, so she moves closer to magnify
The frame has too little pantoscopic tilt for reading
The optical centers are set too wide for near
The add is too strong for her working distance
explanation: A stronger add brings the focal point closer, forcing a short working distance. Eyes On Eyecare warns against setting add power by age alone without considering the patient's tasks and working distance. A reduced add needs the prescriber's approval.

source.title: Eyes On Eyecare: Top 5 Tips for Troubleshooting New Glasses Complaints

stem: A 25-year-old myope gets headaches and eyestrain doing near work in new glasses, though distance is extra crisp. What likely cause should you raise with the prescriber?
choices: Over-minus correction forcing extra accommodation
Under-correction of her myopia, causing squinting
A base curve that's too flat for her prescription
Too much face form inducing prism at near
explanation: Eyes On Eyecare's first tip is not to over-minus myopes: extra minus makes distance look crisp but forces the eyes to accommodate more, producing near-work strain and headaches. The prescriber may cut back the minus or use an anti-fatigue design.

source.title: Eyes On Eyecare: Top 5 Tips for Troubleshooting New Glasses Complaints

stem: Viewed from the front, the patient's right lens sits lower than the left. Her ears are level. What is the correct adjustment?
choices: Angle the right temple down or the left temple up
Angle the right temple up or the left temple down
Shorten the left temple bend so that side sits lower
Bend the right temple inward at the end piece
explanation: Changing tilt on one side is how a crooked front is leveled. Per 20/20's well-adjusted-frame guidance, if the right side is tilted down, increase the pantoscopic tilt on the right (temple angled down, which raises that lens) or reduce it on the left. Then confirm overall tilt is still 5-15°.

source.title: 20/20 Magazine: The Well-Adjusted Frame

topic: Case: One lens closer to the face
stem: Viewed from above, the right lens is closer to the patient's face than the left. Which adjustment corrects this?
choices: Bend the right temple outward at the end piece to open that side
Bend the right temple in at the end piece, or the left out
Increase the pantoscopic tilt on the right side
Shorten the left temple so the left lens moves in
explanation: Per 20/20's guidance, reduce the horizontal angle between the front and the temple on the side that is too close (bringing that temple toward the head), which pushes that lens away from the face. Alternatively, open the angle on the opposite side. Splaying the right temple further would move the right lens even closer.

source.title: 20/20 Magazine: The Well-Adjusted Frame

topic: Case: Sore tops of the ears
stem: Patient says the tops of her ears are sore. You see that the temple bend begins before the top of the ear. What is the best fix?
choices: Bend the temples inward at the hinges
Narrow the nose pads
Move the bend to just past the top of the ear, at about 45°
Increase the bend angle well beyond 45° for more grip
explanation: The temple should curve just above the ear, follow the back of the ear at roughly 45° and avoid excessive pressure on the top or back of the ear. A bend that starts too early rides up on the top of the ear and rubs. Bending more sharply would only increase pressure.

source.title: 20/20 Magazine: The Well-Adjusted Frame

topic: Case: Glasses slide down the nose
stem: Glasses keep sliding down the patient's nose. The temple bend begins well behind the top of the ear, and the tips don't touch the head behind the ear. What is the best fix?
choices: Move the bend to the top of the ear and contour the tip
Lengthen the temples so the tips reach farther behind the ear
Increase the pantoscopic tilt so the frame sits higher
Spread the nose pads apart so the frame sits more securely
explanation: If the bend begins after the top of the ear, the frame can travel forward before the temple catches. 20/20 advises reshaping so the bend conforms at the top of the ear and the tip angles in just enough to touch the head. Spreading the pads or lengthening the temples would make the frame slide more.

source.title: 20/20 Magazine: The Well-Adjusted Frame

topic: Case: Frame resting on the cheeks
stem: A patient with a very flat, low nasal bridge says her metal frame rests on her cheeks. What is the best adjustment?
choices: Shrink the pad-arm loop to minimize vertex distance
Bend the temple tips down behind the ears
Splay the pads nearly parallel and enlarge the pad-arm loop
Increase the pantoscopic tilt
explanation: For very flat bridges, 20/20's well-adjusted-frame article recommends changing the splay angle so the pads sit almost parallel to the face and making the pad-arm loop larger than standard to keep the frame off the lower cheeks. More tilt would push the lower rims into the cheeks.

source.title: 20/20 Magazine: The Well-Adjusted Frame

stem: A patient's new frame tilts so the bottoms of the lenses are farther from her face than the tops. She complains of distortion when she reads. What is the target adjustment?
choices: Increase the vertex distance instead of the tilt
Flatten the face form to 0° to reduce distortion
Increase the retroscopic tilt to about 10°
Create pantoscopic tilt of about 5-15°
explanation: Retroscopic tilt tips the lower lens away from the eye as it rotates down to read, increasing oblique aberrations. NAO's course calls for 5-15° of pantoscopic tilt so the lens stays closer to equidistant from the eye in downgaze, improving field of view and comfort.

source.title: NAO CE: Use SOAP to Solve Eyewear Problems, Part 1

topic: Case: Lens material for a child
stem: A parent asks for CR-39 lenses in her 6-year-old's glasses because they are cheaper. What should you recommend?
choices: Polycarbonate or Trivex for impact resistance
1.74 high index, for the thinnest possible lenses
CR-39 with a scratch coat, since that addresses kids' main risk
Glass, for the best optics and scratch resistance
explanation: 20/20's pediatric dispensing lesson recommends polycarbonate or Trivex for children because they are thin, light, impact resistant and block UV. Active children need impact protection, which scratch coats, glass and standard high-index materials don't provide to the same degree.

source.title: 20/20 Magazine CE: Keys to an Ideal Optical Experience for Kids

stem: A child's temples bow outward from the hinges back to the ears. What does this indicate?
choices: The frame is too wide for the child's head
The temples are too long for the child's ears
The frame front is too narrow
The bridge is too large and sits too low
explanation: Per 20/20's pediatric guidance, temples should run straight from hinge to ear; bowing indicates a frame that is too narrow for the child's head. Temples extending below the ear suggest a frame that is too big. Choose a frame that fits now rather than one to grow into.

source.title: 20/20 Magazine CE: Keys to an Ideal Optical Experience for Kids

topic: Case: Infant's glasses won't stay on
stem: A 14-month-old's glasses won't stay on. Which frame feature does pediatric guidance suggest?
choices: A metal frame with adjustable pads for a secure fit
A bendable nylon frame with an elastic head strap
A rimless mounting so the glasses weigh almost nothing
Spring hinges alone, to keep the temples snug
explanation: 20/20's pediatric lesson describes bendable nylon frames for infants and very young children that include an elastic band around the head to keep the frame in place and add safety. Spring hinges reduce breakage but don't hold a frame on a toddler.

source.title: 20/20 Magazine CE: Keys to an Ideal Optical Experience for Kids

stem: An employer requires high-impact prescription safety eyewear. Which marking should the frame carry under ANSI/ISEA Z87.1-2025?
choices: Z87 U6
explanation: In Z87.1, "Z87-2" identifies prescription eyewear and "+" identifies high-impact certification, so a high-impact Rx frame is marked Z87-2+. Plain Z87 is basic impact, D3 is splash/droplet, and U with a scale number marks UV filtration.

source.title: ANSI Blog: ANSI/ISEA Z87.1-2025 Safety Glasses

topic: Case: Dress glasses as safety glasses
stem: A machinist asks if his everyday polycarbonate dress glasses count as workplace safety eyewear. What is the best answer?
choices: Yes, as long as the lenses are at least 2 mm thick at center
Yes, if the frame has spring hinges and side shields added
No; occupational eyewear must meet and be marked to ANSI Z87.1
Yes; all polycarbonate glasses qualify as workplace safety eyewear
explanation: Every dress lens must pass the FDA impact requirement (21 CFR 801.410), but that is not the same as occupational protection. ANSI Z87.1 safety eyewear carries Z87 markings (Z87-2 for Rx, + for high impact) on qualifying components. Lens material alone doesn't make a dress frame a safety device.

source.title: ANSI Blog: ANSI/ISEA Z87.1-2025 Safety Glasses

stem: You are dispensing prescription glass lenses. Which FDA impact-testing requirement applies?
choices: Glass prescription lenses are exempt from testing
Only lenses stronger than 3.00 D are tested
Only a statistical sample from each batch is tested
Each finished glass lens must be individually drop-ball tested
explanation: 21 CFR 801.410 requires that each finished impact-resistant glass lens for prescription use be individually tested (a 5/8-inch steel ball dropped from 50 inches). Batch sampling applies to manufacturers of other lenses, such as plastic.

source.title: eCFR: 21 CFR 801.410 Impact-resistant lenses

stem: A doctor wants a patient to have a lens that isn't impact resistant. What does FDA regulation require?
choices: The doctor directs other lenses in writing and notifies the patient in writing
Nothing, because the doctor can simply request it by phone
The optician notes the exception in the patient's chart
The patient signs a waiver at the dispensing table, kept on file for 3 years
explanation: 21 CFR 801.410 allows an exception only when the physician or optometrist finds that impact-resistant lenses will not fulfill the patient's visual requirements, directs in writing the use of other lenses and gives written notice to the patient. A dispensing-table waiver doesn't meet the rule.

source.title: eCFR: 21 CFR 801.410 Impact-resistant lenses

stem: Patient says: "My photochromic lenses barely darken when I drive." What explains this, and what can you offer?
choices: Windshields block most UV; offer a car-activating lens or Rx sunglasses
Heat inside the car keeps them clear; keep the cabin cool and they'll darken
Photochromics need a few weeks of sun exposure to fully break in
The lenses are defective and need to be remade under warranty
explanation: Most photochromic lenses react primarily to UV, and car windshields block most UV, so they don't darken enough in the car. Transitions notes that XTRActive responds to both UV and visible light and can darken behind the windshield; Drivewear is designed for driving. Dedicated Rx sunglasses are the other option.

source.title: Transitions: How Do Photochromics Work?

stem: A skier says her photochromic lenses take a long time to clear after she comes indoors on cold days. What is the best explanation?
choices: The lenses have lost their photochromic dye and need replacing
Snow reflects infrared light that keeps the lenses dark indoors
The AR coating is trapping UV inside the lens material
Cold slows the molecules, so fading back to clear takes longer
explanation: Transitions explains that the molecules move slowly when cold, so lenses take longer to go from dark to clear, while warm lenses fade back faster. This is normal behavior, not a defect.

source.title: Transitions: How Do Photochromics Work?

stem: A driver with new polarized sunglasses says his dashboard display and phone screen look dark or hard to read at certain angles. What is the best explanation?
choices: Polarizers can dim LCD screens at some angles; this is expected
The lenses need AR on the front to stop screen reflections
The polarizing film is delaminating and the lenses should be remade
A photochromic layer is activating from the screen's light
explanation: LCD screens emit polarized light, so a polarizing filter can dim or black them out depending on the angle. Consumer guidance notes polarized lenses can make dashboards, phones, ATMs and some watches harder to read and icy patches harder to see. Discuss this before dispensing to pilots and heavy screen users.

source.title: PrimeVision: Polarized vs Photochromic Lenses

topic: Case: Pattern near polarized lens edges
stem: In some lighting a patient notices an irregular pattern near the edges of her polarized lenses. What should you check?
choices: Too much pantoscopic tilt bending light unevenly through the film near the edges
Lens stress; check with a polariscope for tight screws or oversized lenses
Incorrect add power showing through the polarized film
Excess UV transmission causing the film to fade unevenly
explanation: Polarized lenses can reveal their own stress pattern. 20/20 recommends checking with a colmascope or polariscope (a polarized laptop screen can substitute) and making sure screws aren't over-tightened and lenses weren't edged too large or bent.

source.title: 20/20 Magazine: Twenty Essential Troubleshooting Tips for Opticians

topic: Case: White rim on polarized lenses
stem: Patient notices a light, whitish rim around the edge of her polarized lenses, especially at the top. What is the best fix on the remake?
choices: Order a mirror coating
Use a back-surface bevel so more lens shows in front
Order a thicker polarizing film
Bevel closer to the front, and tint or color the lens edge
explanation: The color of a polarized lens comes from the film; the plastic in front of and behind it is clear, so an exposed edge looks white. 20/20 recommends moving the bevel toward the front so less edge protrudes and tinting the edge on tintable materials (color pens for polycarbonate).

source.title: 20/20 Magazine: Twenty Essential Troubleshooting Tips for Opticians

stem: A TV reporter in new 1.67 high-index lenses says viewers can't see her eyes because of reflections. What is the best recommendation?
choices: A polished edge bevel so the lens looks clearer and thinner
A polarized lens to block the studio lights' reflections
A light gray tint so reflections are less noticeable on camera
AR treatment, since reflectance rises with refractive index
explanation: Darryl Meister explains in 20/20 that reflectance of a lens surface increases with refractive index, and that reflections obscure the wearer's eyes and facial expressions. High-index lenses especially need AR. A tint or a polished edge would add to the cosmetic problem.

source.title: 20/20 Magazine: The Evolution of Anti-Reflective Coatings, Part 1

topic: Case: Ghost images while night driving
stem: A patient says that at night he sees ghost images and halos around headlights through his uncoated lenses. Which lens option targets this?
choices: A quality anti-reflective coating
Polarized lenses to cut headlight glare
Photochromic lenses that adjust to headlights
A yellow night-driving tint to sharpen contrast
explanation: 20/20's multiple-pairs lesson notes that night-driving lenses should have quality AR coatings that reduce surface and internal reflections, which cause ghost images and halos. Tints reduce light reaching the eye at night, and photochromic or polarized lenses don't address reflections at night.

source.title: 20/20 Magazine CE: Multiple Pairs - Every Job Needs the Right Tool

stem: A patient with -6.00 D high-index lenses complains the temporal edges are still very thick. Her PD is 58 mm, and the frame's distance between centers is 72 mm. What is the main cause?
choices: Large decentration: the frame center distance far exceeds her PD
A base curve that's too steep, adding edge thickness all around
Too much pantoscopic tilt, which thickens the temporal edge
The lab used a lower index than ordered, so every edge came out thicker
explanation: When the PD is much smaller than the frame's DBC, each lens is decentered inward and the temporal edge of a minus lens gets thicker. 20/20 advises matching DBC and PD more closely and watching corner shapes. High index helps, but it can't overcome 7 mm of decentration per lens.

source.title: 20/20 Magazine: Twenty Essential Troubleshooting Tips for Opticians

topic: Case: Chipping in a grooved rimless
stem: Low-power CR-39 lenses (+0.25 -0.25 × 180) in a grooved rimless frame are chipping at the groove. What is the best solution?
choices: Thicker edges (about 2.2-2.5 mm) or polycarbonate/Trivex
Glass lenses, which are harder than plastic and resist chipping at the groove
Thinner edges to reduce weight and stress at the groove
Move the groove toward the back edge to reduce stress
explanation: Stock finished lenses can be too thin at the edge for the groove plus enough wall to resist chipping. 20/20 cites about 2.4 mm as the right edge thickness, recommends telling the lab the frame is grooved rimless, and suggests polycarbonate or Trivex for their anti-chip properties when thinner edges are wanted.

source.title: 20/20 Magazine: Twenty Essential Troubleshooting Tips for Opticians

topic: Case: Magnified eyes in high plus
stem: A +6.00 D patient dislikes how her eyes look magnified and how her lenses bulge out of the frame. What is the best lens recommendation?
choices: Spherical CR-39 on a steeper base curve
Aspheric high-index lenses
A larger frame with more decentration
Polarized lenses
explanation: Flatter aspheric fronts reduce magnification and bulge, and high index reduces center thickness. 20/20 recommends a lens that is both aspheric and high-index so the eyewire keeps its shape and the eyes look more natural. A steeper spherical lens and a larger, decentered frame both add thickness.

source.title: 20/20 Magazine: Twenty Essential Troubleshooting Tips for Opticians

stem: Using the formula MBS = effective diameter + 2 × decentration, find the minimum blank for a frame with an ED of 58 mm and 3 mm of decentration per lens.
choices: 61 mm
64 mm
70 mm
58 mm
explanation: Per 20/20's tip, MBS = ED + 2 × decentration = 58 + 2(3) = 64 mm. Many labs also add a couple of millimeters for edging allowance, but the formula answer is 64 mm, so a 75 mm stock blank has plenty of room.

source.title: 20/20 Magazine: Twenty Essential Troubleshooting Tips for Opticians

stem: Two opticians read the same lens on the same manual lensmeter and get different powers. What should each do first?
choices: Read only the sphere and ignore cylinder
Average their two readings
Turn the power drum rapidly back and forth to find focus
Focus the eyepiece for their own eye with the drum at zero
explanation: 20/20 recommends each optician set the drum to plano and focus the eyepiece until the target is crisp for their own eye. It also warns against turning the drum back and forth, because the reader's own accommodation then skews the reading.

source.title: 20/20 Magazine: Twenty Essential Troubleshooting Tips for Opticians

topic: Case: Can't find the OC horizontally
stem: Verifying a +1.00 -1.00 × 090 lens, you can't locate the optical center horizontally to check the PD. Why, and how should you judge acceptance?
choices: The cylinder axis was ground wrong, so remake before checking
Use the sphere power with Prentice's rule to compute horizontal prism
The 180° meridian is plano, so check vertical imbalance instead
The lens is defective because every lens has a horizontal OC
explanation: With axis 090, the 90° meridian carries the sphere (+1.00) and the 180° meridian carries sphere plus cylinder (0.00). With no horizontal power, decentration creates no horizontal prism. 20/20 suggests using other reference points, confirming vertical imbalance is within tolerance and applying the 0.66Δ horizontal limit.

source.title: 20/20 Magazine: Twenty Essential Troubleshooting Tips for Opticians

stem: A pair of -2.00 D OU single-vision lenses shows 0.50Δ of vertical imbalance at the PRPs. Under ANSI Z80.1-2015, what do you do?
choices: Accept: the vertical tolerance is 1.0Δ
Accept: it is within 0.67Δ
Accept: vertical prism isn't toleranced for single vision
Reject: it exceeds the 0.33Δ vertical tolerance
explanation: For powers up to ±3.375 D, ANSI Z80.1-2015 allows no more than 0.33Δ of vertical imbalance; above that, the PRP heights may differ by no more than 1.0 mm. The 0.67Δ figure is the horizontal tolerance. Vertical is held tighter because the eyes fuse vertical differences poorly.

source.title: The Vision Council: ANSI Z80.1-2015 Quick Reference Guide

topic: Case: Horizontal PD on a stronger Rx
stem: Rx is -5.00 D OU with an ordered PD of 64 mm. The optical centers measure 62 mm apart. Under ANSI Z80.1-2015, what do you do?
choices: Reject: the PD must be within 1.0 mm at this power
Accept: horizontal prism is not toleranced in single vision
Accept: it is within ±2.5 mm of the specified PD
Reject: the induced 1.0Δ exceeds the 0.67Δ limit
explanation: For single-vision and multifocal lenses stronger than ±2.75 D, ANSI switches from a 0.67Δ limit to a distance rule: the OCs must be within ±2.5 mm of the specified distance PD. A 2 mm error passes, even though it produces 1.0Δ. The 1.0 mm figure applies to each monocular PAL fitting cross.

source.title: The Vision Council: ANSI Z80.1-2015 Quick Reference Guide

stem: Progressives were ordered at 21 mm fitting height OU. On inspection, the right fitting cross is at 20 mm and the left at 22 mm. Under ANSI Z80.1-2015, what do you do?
choices: Accept: each lens is individually within ±1.0 mm of the order
Accept: PAL fitting heights are toleranced at ±2.5 mm
Reject: the heights differ by 2 mm, over the 1.0 mm limit
Reject: each lens must match the ordered height exactly
explanation: ANSI requires each fitting cross to be within ±1.0 mm of the ordered height and the difference between the two mounted lenses to be no more than 1.0 mm. Each lens passes individually, but the 2 mm difference fails, and an unequal pair is what causes asymmetric zones.

source.title: The Vision Council: ANSI Z80.1-2015 Quick Reference Guide

stem: A lens ordered as -1.00 cylinder at axis 180 reads at axis 177. Under ANSI Z80.1-2015, what do you do?
choices: Reject: the tolerance for this cylinder is ±2°
Reject: the tolerance for all cylinder powers is ±1°
Accept: the tolerance for this cylinder is ±3°
Accept: the tolerance for any cylinder under 2.00 D is ±7°
explanation: ANSI tolerances tighten as cylinder increases: ±7° for >0.25 to 0.50 D, ±5° for >0.50 to 0.75 D, ±3° for >0.75 to 1.50 D, and ±2° above 1.50 D. A -1.00 cylinder is allowed ±3°, so 177 passes.

source.title: The Vision Council: ANSI Z80.1-2015 Quick Reference Guide

topic: Case: Neck strain at the computer
stem: A presbyope in general-purpose progressives works at a desktop monitor most of the day and complains of neck strain from tipping her head back. What is the best recommendation?
choices: A stronger add in her general PALs so the screen is clearer
Raise the PAL fitting height 4 mm to bring the intermediate up
An office/computer lens as a dedicated task pair
Single-vision distance lenses with the monitor moved closer
explanation: 20/20's multiple-pairs lesson recommends office and computer lenses for patients who spend many hours at a screen: they give a wide intermediate and near field positioned so the wearer keeps a natural posture, reducing neck and head strain. Raising a general PAL disrupts distance vision.

source.title: 20/20 Magazine CE: Multiple Pairs - Every Job Needs the Right Tool

stem: A patient is upgrading from bifocals to trifocals. As a starting point, where is the trifocal segment top usually placed?
choices: At the lower edge of the pupil
At the center of the pupil
At the lower lid margin, like a bifocal
About 2 mm below the lower lid margin
explanation: 20/20's segment-height guidance: fit bifocals to the top of the lower lid and trifocals to the lower edge of the pupil, measuring from the lowest edge of the lens. Then refine for the previous pair, the patient's height and how the glasses will be used.

source.title: 20/20 Magazine: Segment Height

stem: A golfer wants a second pair of flat-top bifocals for the course because the segment gets in the way when he putts. How should the segment height compare with his everyday pair?
choices: Fit it much lower
Fit it higher
Keep the same height and add pantoscopic tilt
Keep the same height with a wider segment
explanation: 20/20 notes that a second pair for golf should be fit much lower so the segment isn't in the way when putting. By contrast, tall patients who use eyewear standing may need 1-2 mm lower, and reading-only pairs can be fit higher.

source.title: 20/20 Magazine: Segment Height

stem: A motorcyclist wants one wrapped, polarized progressive pair for everything. What does dispensing guidance suggest considering?
choices: Photochromic progressives, which darken best behind a visor
Flat-top bifocals in an 8-base wrap
A distance-only riding pair plus progressives in a dress pair
Standard progressives in a flat frame
explanation: 20/20 suggests determining the lens use first: a motorcyclist may get better results with distance vision in a dedicated riding pair and a progressive in a dress pair, presenting the riding eyewear as safety equipment. Photochromics don't darken well behind UV-blocking shields.

source.title: 20/20 Magazine: Twenty Essential Troubleshooting Tips for Opticians

stem: A patient's Rx is unchanged, but she switched from CR-39 to 1.67 high index for thinness. Now she reports dizziness and discomfort. Measurements match the old pair. What is the most likely contributor?
choices: A missing UV block in the high-index material
An incorrect PD, since thinner lenses need a different PD
The material change and the base-curve change with it
An incorrect add power ordered on the new pair
explanation: 20/20's remake-prevention lesson warns that sudden material switches, such as CR-39 to polycarbonate or 1.67, can cause dizziness, headaches and discomfort linked to the accompanying base-curve change. Match materials carefully or prepare the patient for adaptation.

source.title: 20/20 Magazine CE: Tips to Decrease Remakes, Part 2

topic: Case: Fitting crosses high in an acetate frame
stem: In an acetate frame without adjustable pads, the remarked progressive fitting crosses sit about 1 mm above the pupil centers. Which adjustment lowers them relative to the pupils?
choices: Increase the face form
Increase the pantoscopic tilt
Narrow the temple spread
Decrease the pantoscopic tilt
explanation: 20/20's Problem Solving 101 notes that in an acetate frame, increasing pantoscopic tilt lowers a fitting cross that is too high (and makes the reading area easier to reach), while decreasing tilt raises it. Larger errors still need a remake with correct heights.

source.title: 20/20 Magazine CE: Problem Solving 101

stem: A new optician measured progressive fitting heights on a frame straight off the display, then adjusted it at dispensing. The patient now says the heights feel wrong. What should have been done?
choices: Measure the heights with the patient looking down
Measure only a binocular PD
Add 2 mm to every measured height
Adjust the frame to the patient before measuring heights
explanation: 20/20's segment-height guidance makes frame adjustment the first step: about 5° of face form and 7-10° of pantoscopic tilt, with a short vertex distance, before measuring heights. Adjusting afterward moves the frame on the face and shifts the fitting crosses away from the pupils.

source.title: 20/20 Magazine: Segment Height

stem: A patient reports distortion in a new single-vision lens. In the lensmeter you find unexpected cylinder, and the lens measures one base curve horizontally and another vertically. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The PD was measured incorrectly, inducing cylinder
The cylinder axis was set wrong when the lens was surfaced
The AR coating is crazing and distorting the surface
The lens was edged too large and is warped in the eyewire
explanation: NAO describes warping from incorrect sizing during finishing: a lens forced into an eyewire that is too small measures different curves in different meridians, creating unwanted cylinder and distortion. The fix is to remake it at the correct size.

source.title: NAO CE: Use SOAP to Solve Eyewear Problems, Part 2

stem: At follow-up, a soft lens barely moves on blink or upgaze, there is a ring of conjunctival indentation at the lens edge, and the patient says vision is a bit hazy but clears for a moment right after each blink. Comfort was good at first. What is the interpretation and change?
choices: Tight fit: flatten the base curve or reduce the diameter
Ideal fit: no change needed
Loose fit: steepen the base curve or enlarge the diameter
Inverted lens: remove and reinsert it
explanation: Contamac's soft lens chapter lists the steep/tight picture: movement under 0.25 mm, conjunctival indentation or injection, initially good comfort and vision that improves briefly after the blink. A tight lens is loosened with a smaller diameter or flatter base curve (or a less rigid material). Tight lenses limit tear exchange.

source.title: Contamac In-Contact, Chapter 10: Fitting Soft Contact Lenses

stem: A soft lens decenters, moves more than 1 mm on blink, shows edge fluting, and the patient says vision is sharp just after a blink and then blurs. Comfort is poor. What is the best change?
choices: Flatten the base curve or decrease the diameter
Steepen the base curve or increase the diameter
Switch to a higher-water, more flexible material
Leave it; movement over 1 mm is ideal
explanation: Per Contamac, a flat/loose lens shows excess movement (over 1 mm), poor centration, possible edge stand-off or fluting, poor comfort and vision that sharpens just after the blink and then blurs. To tighten it, choose a larger diameter, a steeper base curve, or a more rigid/lower-water material.

source.title: Contamac In-Contact, Chapter 10: Fitting Soft Contact Lenses

stem: During keratometry over a soft lens, the mires are clear immediately after a blink, then become distorted and blurry. What does this suggest?
choices: A loose (flat) lens
An inverted lens
A tight (steep) lens
Normal tear-film breakup only
explanation: Contamac describes this for a steep fit: irregular mires that briefly clear after the blink, when the blink momentarily pushes the vaulted lens against the cornea, then distort again. A loose lens shows the opposite visual pattern, blurring after the blink as it slides.

source.title: Contamac In-Contact, Chapter 10: Fitting Soft Contact Lenses

stem: Two minutes after inserting a new silicone hydrogel trial lens, it looks slightly loose. What is appropriate?
choices: Let it settle about 20 minutes before judging the fit
Steepen the base curve right away to tighten it
Judge it now; silicone hydrogels don't change after insertion
Increase the diameter right away to improve centration
explanation: Soft lens movement decreases over the first 20-25 minutes. Contamac notes that a 5-minute assessment can predict fit for traditional hydrogels, but silicone hydrogels may need closer to 20 minutes to settle before the fit can be reliably assessed. Changing parameters too early risks refitting a lens that would have settled.

source.title: Contamac In-Contact, Chapter 10: Fitting Soft Contact Lenses

stem: A soft lens is slightly tight. According to soft lens fitting guidance, which parameter change usually has the larger effect?
choices: Reducing the diameter, which influences fit more than base curve
Flattening the base curve, which guidance says should always be changed first
Increasing the center thickness to stiffen the lens
Changing the power, since higher minus lenses fit tighter
explanation: Contamac notes that corneal diameter plays a more significant role in soft lens fit than base curve, so diameter should be changed first for a meaningful effect; roughly, a 0.50 mm diameter change equals a 0.20 mm base curve change. Power and thickness have only minor effects on fit.

source.title: Contamac In-Contact, Chapter 10: Fitting Soft Contact Lenses

topic: Case: Toric rotation to the left
stem: A right-eye soft toric for -1.25 × 180 settles with its marker rotated 10° to your left as you face the patient, and vision is blurry. Using LARS, what axis should you order?
explanation: LARS means Left Add, Right Subtract, judged from the examiner's view. A 10° rotation to the left is added to the prescribed axis: 180 + 10 = 190, written as 010. Ordering the compensated axis lets the lens's stable resting position put the cylinder where the eye needs it.

source.title: Contact Lens Spectrum: Troubleshooting Toric Soft Lenses

topic: Case: Toric rotation to the right
stem: A soft toric with a prescription axis of 090 settles with its marker rotated 15° to your right. Using LARS, which axis should you order?
explanation: With LARS (Left Add, Right Subtract), rotation to the examiner's right is subtracted: 90 - 15 = 75. Contact Lens Spectrum recommends reordering with a revised allowance for the observed rotation once the lens shows a stable, repeatable position.

source.title: Contact Lens Spectrum: Troubleshooting Toric Soft Lenses

stem: A toric lens's 6 o'clock marker rests at the 7 o'clock position. Using the clock-face method, about how much rotation is this?
explanation: A clock face has 12 hours spanning 360°, so each hour equals 30°. GPLI's pocket guide describes estimating toric rotation with the slit-lamp degree scale or this clock approach, then applying LARS to find the final axis.

source.title: GPLI: Contact Lens Clinical Pearls Pocket Guide

stem: A soft toric lens moves excessively, its markings sit in a different position from blink to blink, and vision fluctuates. What is the most likely cause?
choices: Cylinder power too low
Base curve too steep (tight fit)
Lens too thin to stabilize
Base curve too flat (loose fit)
explanation: Contact Lens Spectrum notes that a back optic zone radius that is too flat gives excessive movement and an unstable, inconsistent orientation, so the cylinder axis keeps shifting. A steep lens can also blur vision, but by vaulting the corneal apex, not by spinning. Correct the fit before changing the axis.

source.title: Contact Lens Spectrum: Troubleshooting Toric Soft Lenses

stem: A soft toric wearer has blurred vision. A spherocylindrical over-refraction restores the expected acuity, and its spherical equivalent is zero. What does this indicate?
choices: Lens rotation, not a sphere or cylinder power error
Ocular pathology, so the patient needs medical referral
A sphere power error, so the lens needs a new sphere
A cylinder power error, so the lens needs more cylinder
explanation: Contact Lens Spectrum explains that a rotated toric lens produces a crossed-cylinder over-refraction whose spherical equivalent is zero, because the lens and ocular spherical equivalents still cancel regardless of axis. A nonzero spherical equivalent points to a power error. Improved acuity rules out pathology as the main cause.

source.title: Contact Lens Spectrum: Troubleshooting Toric Soft Lenses

stem: A CooperVision multifocal wearer says near is fine but distance could be sharper. Per the manufacturer's fitting guide, what is the first adjustment?
choices: Switch both eyes to the N design for a smoother transition
Add +0.25 D to the non-dominant eye to balance the pair
Trial ±0.25 D on the dominant eye, then confirm near holds
Lower the add power in both eyes until distance is clear
explanation: CooperVision's guide says: do not change the add power. To enhance distance, offer ±0.25 D to the dominant eye with handheld lenses or a flipper; if distance improves, check that near is maintained, then adjust that eye's sphere. Near is fine-tuned on the non-dominant eye.

source.title: CooperVision: Multifocal Contact Lens Fitting Guides

stem: A CooperVision multifocal wearer has good distance vision but wants better near. Per the manufacturer's fitting guide, what is the approach?
choices: Increase the add one step in both eyes, since the near zone is underpowered
Refit as monovision right away, since multifocals failed
Trial ±0.25 D on the non-dominant eye, then confirm distance holds
Add -0.25 D to the dominant eye so it accommodates more
explanation: CooperVision's optimization step for near: offer ±0.25 D to the non-dominant eye; if near improves, check that distance holds and adjust that eye's sphere. The guide explicitly says not to change the add power, which also alters the distance optics.

source.title: CooperVision: Multifocal Contact Lens Fitting Guides

stem: A new multifocal wearer reads the chart one minute after insertion and declares the lenses a failure. What is the best response?
choices: Switch her to monovision immediately to avoid a long adaptation
Increase the add power immediately, since near is usually the issue
Refit single-vision lenses with readers, since she isn't a candidate
Have her wear them outside the room 10-15 minutes, then reassess
explanation: CooperVision's guide has wearers experience their vision outside the testing room for 10-15 minutes before assessment, and Contact Lens Spectrum advises that multifocal fits shouldn't be declared a success or failure on the initial fitting day. Real-world targets (phones, labels) are more meaningful than a chart in the first minute.

source.title: CooperVision: Multifocal Contact Lens Fitting Guides

stem: Before fitting CooperVision multifocals, how does the manufacturer's guide have you determine ocular dominance?
choices: A hole-in-card test, with dominance confirmed by acuity
Whichever eye has the better acuity on the chart
Whichever eye has the higher prescription, since it needs priority
+1.00 D blur method: the eye more bothered by blur is dominant
explanation: Step 1 of CooperVision's multifocal guide is to determine dominance with the +1.00 D blur method: hold a +1.00 lens over each eye in turn while the patient views a distance target; the eye that is more bothered by the blur is dominant and gets the distance-biased lens.

source.title: CooperVision: Multifocal Contact Lens Fitting Guides

topic: Case: Small pupils with a center-distance multifocal
stem: An older presbyope with small pupils struggles at near in a center-distance concentric multifocal. Why, and what design may help?
choices: The lens is too tight; flatten the base curve
The near zone falls outside her small pupil; try center-near
Her pupils are too large; try a center-distance design
Her add is too low; raise it two steps
explanation: Contact Lens Spectrum explains that older presbyopes typically have smaller pupils, so with a center-distance concentric design the near zone sits outside the pupil during near work. Center-near aspheric designs put the add over the visual axis as the pupil constricts.

source.title: Contact Lens Spectrum: Fine-Tune Your Multifocal Lens Fitting

stem: When refining soft multifocal powers, which principle is recommended?
choices: Always use the full age-based add
Most plus acceptable at distance, least add needed at near
Use equal distance and add powers in both eyes
Use the most minus at distance and the highest add
explanation: Contact Lens Spectrum advises pushing the highest plus acceptable at distance and the least plus at near, to avoid excessive accommodation and adaptation problems from too high an add. Refraction accuracy and sphere adjustments come before add changes.

source.title: Contact Lens Spectrum: Fine-Tune Your Multifocal Lens Fitting

stem: A monovision wearer says judging distances is harder, especially when driving at night. What does monovision commonly cause, and what is a safer driving option?
choices: Reduced stereopsis; full distance correction for driving
Increased stereopsis; no change is needed
Corneal hypoxia; switch to silicone hydrogel
Lens decentration; refit with larger lenses
explanation: Review of Optometry notes that monovision often reduces near stereopsis, affecting depth perception, and higher adds can blur all distances or cause double vision. Distance correction in both eyes (with readers for near) is described as the safer option for driving.

source.title: Review of Optometry: Monovision vs. Multifocal

stem: A translating GP bifocal slips under the lower lid on downgaze instead of being pushed up, so near vision is poor. What adjustment is suggested?
choices: Reduce the add power so near is easier to reach
Decrease the diameter by 1 mm to reduce lid contact
Flatten the base curve or the peripheral curves
Steepen the base curve so the lens rides higher
explanation: A translating lens must rest on the lower lid and be pushed up as the eye looks down. Contact Lens Spectrum says that if the lens is too tight and moves below the lower lid instead of being moved up by it, flatten the base curve or peripheral curves. The lower lid also needs to be near the lower limbus.

source.title: Contact Lens Spectrum: Fine-Tune Your Multifocal Lens Fitting

stem: A GP wearer shows punctate staining at 3 and 9 o'clock and complains of lens awareness and dryness. Which management fits?
choices: Switch to extended wear so the cornea stays covered at night
Improve centration, decrease edge lift, and encourage blinking and drops
Leave it, since 3 and 9 staining rarely progresses or matters
Increase the edge lift substantially so more tears flow under the lens edge
explanation: GPLI attributes 3 and 9 staining to desiccation of the exposed cornea, aggravated by dryness and lid margin disease. Management includes improving centration, decreasing edge lift, proper blinking, rewetting drops, lid hygiene and a humidifier. Untreated, it can progress to opacification and neovascularization.

source.title: GPLI: GP Lens Management Guide, page 9

stem: A GP lens drops quickly from the upper lid and rides low; fluorescein shows only a thin peripheral band. Which design change improves lid attachment?
choices: Steepen the base curve by 1.00 D
Reduce the overall diameter
Increase the edge lift
Decrease the edge lift
explanation: Contact Lens Spectrum explains that too little edge lift makes a lens lid-attach poorly and ride low, while excessive edge lift makes it lid-attach too well and ride high. Standard designs carry about 0.10-0.13 mm of edge lift, and a change of about 0.03 mm makes a noticeable difference.

source.title: Contact Lens Spectrum: GP Insights (edge lift), April 2005

stem: A GP lens rides high, strongly lid-attached, with a wide peripheral fluorescein band. Which change helps?
choices: Decrease the edge lift
Add a minus lenticular edge
Increase the edge lift
Flatten the base curve
explanation: Excess edge lift (a wide peripheral pattern) lets the upper lid grab the lens too well, so it rides high. Contact Lens Spectrum recommends adjusting edge lift in about 0.03 mm steps. A minus lenticular or a flatter base curve would increase lid attachment and upward positioning.

source.title: Contact Lens Spectrum: GP Insights (edge lift), April 2005

stem: A GP trial lens shows central fluorescein pooling with a trapped bubble. What is the interpretation?
choices: Alignment fit: no change needed
Flat fit: steepen the base curve
Steep fit: flatten the base curve
Too much edge lift: decrease it
explanation: GPLI's pocket guide: flat fits show central touch with edge pooling, and steep fits show central pooling and bubbles. Use the cobalt filter with a yellow Wratten filter for best evaluation, and aim for alignment, often on or slightly flatter than flat K.

source.title: GPLI: Contact Lens Clinical Pearls Pocket Guide

stem: You want to flatten a GP fit without changing the base curve radius. Which change accomplishes this?
choices: Decrease the optical zone diameter
Increase the center thickness
Increase the optical zone diameter
Switch to a higher-Dk material
explanation: Per GPLI, increasing the optical zone diameter increases sagittal depth and steepens the fit, while decreasing it reduces sagittal depth and flattens the fit. Thickness and Dk changes affect flexure and oxygen, not the fitting relationship.

source.title: GPLI: Contact Lens Clinical Pearls Pocket Guide

stem: A GP wearer with high corneal astigmatism has vision that varies with the blink. Over-keratometry shows toricity, yet the lens measures spherical on the radiuscope. What is the likely cause and management?
choices: A tight fit: enlarge the optic zone
Residual lenticular astigmatism: add front cylinder
A warped lens: replace it with the same parameters
Flexure: add center thickness or flatten the base curve
explanation: GPLI lists flexure as causing vision that varies with the blink, diagnosed by toricity on over-keratometry with a spherical radiuscope reading. Causes include high astigmatism, steep base curves, thin designs and large optic zones; management includes a flatter base curve, more center thickness, a smaller OZD or a lower-Dk material.

source.title: GPLI: GP Lens Management Guide, page 9

stem: An extended-wear GP patient wakes with an immobile lens, an indentation ring and mild awareness. What is the management?
choices: Extend overnight wear gradually to build corneal tolerance
Decrease the edge lift so the lens seals better and stops moving overnight
Steepen the base curve so the lens centers better overnight
Flatten the peripheral curve, go to daily wear, use drops on waking
explanation: GPLI lists dryness, decentration, back-surface deposits, peripheral seal-off and extended wear with low edge lift as causes of adherence. Management: improve centration, clean the back surface, flatten the peripheral curve, reduce to daily wear and use rewetting drops upon awakening and at night. Steepening or lowering edge lift would worsen seal-off.

source.title: GPLI: GP Lens Management Guide, page 10

stem: A GP wearer's vision has gradually hazed, and the lens surface beads up. She uses a lotion-containing hand soap before handling her lenses. What is the best advice?
choices: Sleep in the lenses so they stay hydrated and wet better
Rinse the lenses with tap water each morning to wash off the surface film
Store the lenses dry overnight so the film evaporates
Re-educate on cleaning; avoid lanolin soaps before handling
explanation: GPLI lists poor cleaning compliance, lanolin-containing soap or lotion, poorly wettable materials and inadequate tears as causes of poor acquired wettability. Management includes re-education, avoiding lanolin products before handling, weekly enzymatic cleaning or a material change. Tap water is never acceptable for lenses.

source.title: GPLI: GP Lens Management Guide, page 10

topic: Case: GP glare from low riding
stem: A GP wearer reports glare and vision that varies with the blink; the lens rides low, so she often looks through the lens periphery. Which approach addresses this?
choices: Reduce the overall diameter by 1 mm so it rides higher
Use a higher specific-gravity material so the lens settles more stably on the lid
Improve centration, e.g., flatter BCR, thinner center, lenticular edge
Accept it; glare means the optic zone is centered over the pupil
explanation: GPLI lists varying vision and awareness from looking through the non-optical periphery as signs of decentration. For inferior decentration, it recommends lenticular designs by power (plus lenticular for powers stronger than -5.00, minus lenticular for low minus and plus), a flatter BCR, minimized CT and a lower specific-gravity material.

source.title: GPLI: GP Lens Management Guide, page 9

stem: A GP lens consistently decenters temporally. Per GPLI's management guide, which changes help?
choices: A thicker center
A higher specific-gravity material
A larger overall diameter and a steeper base curve
A smaller overall diameter and a flatter base curve
explanation: GPLI's management for lateral decentration is a larger overall diameter, a steeper BCR or an aspheric design. These increase the lens's hold on the cornea; a smaller, flatter lens would decenter more.

source.title: GPLI: GP Lens Management Guide, page 9

stem: A patient who sleeps in his soft lenses wakes with one very red eye and mild irritation; there is little or no corneal staining. What is the most likely condition and action?
choices: Normal morning redness that clears within an hour
Allergic conjunctivitis: continue wear with antihistamine drops
An inverted lens: remove, flip and reinsert it
CLARE: remove lenses, stop wear and refer promptly
explanation: Contact Lens Spectrum describes CLARE as a unilateral acute red eye on waking in someone sleeping in lenses, with minimal staining: an inflammatory response to gram-negative bacteria. Temporarily ceasing wear should bring significant resolution in a day or two; any contact lens red eye needs the doctor's evaluation to rule out infection.

source.title: Contact Lens Spectrum: Practical Red Eye Problem-Solving

topic: Case: Peripheral infiltrate after overnight wear
stem: After overnight wear, a patient has a small, round, peripheral corneal infiltrate with overlying epithelial loss and only mild discomfort. What is the best action?
choices: Continue wear with rewetting drops and recheck next month
Suspect CLPU: stop wear and refer for close follow-up
Switch to a new solution brand and keep wearing as usual
Refit with a tighter lens to reduce peripheral movement
explanation: Contact Lens Spectrum describes CLPU as small, round, peripheral infiltrates with overlying epithelial loss, often unilateral and after overnight wear, linked to gram-positive bacteria. Management is temporary discontinuation, close monitoring for 24-48 hours, and often a precautionary antibiotic from the doctor.

source.title: Contact Lens Spectrum: Practical Red Eye Problem-Solving

topic: Case: Painful red eye with a central spot
stem: A soft lens wearer calls with increasing eye pain, light sensitivity, discharge and blurred vision; she can see a white spot near the center of her cornea. What is the best action?
choices: Patch the eye overnight and reassess in the morning
Switch to a fresh pair of lenses and see if it settles
Remove the lenses and get same-day care from the eye doctor
Use rewetting drops for a day and recheck next week if no better
explanation: These are the features of microbial keratitis: a central lesion often 2 mm or larger, a hot painful eye, photophobia and discharge. Contact Lens Spectrum calls it an ocular emergency requiring aggressive therapy. Lens wear stops immediately; patching a contact lens-related eye is dangerous.

source.title: Contact Lens Spectrum: Practical Red Eye Problem-Solving

topic: Case: Tap-water rinsing and severe pain
stem: A wearer who rinses his lenses and case with tap water now has severe eye pain. Which infection is of particular concern, and what should he do?
choices: GPC, managed by switching to daily disposables
Acanthamoeba keratitis: stop wear and refer urgently
CLARE, which resolves without treatment
Solution toxicity, managed by switching to peroxide
explanation: CDC notes that Acanthamoeba is commonly found in tap, lake and well water and can cause a very painful keratitis that may need a year or more of treatment and can lead to transplant or blindness. Water exposure is the key risk factor, and a severely painful eye in this setting needs urgent medical care.

source.title: CDC: Keeping Water Away from Contact Lenses

stem: When teaching a new wearer, which symptoms should you say mean remove the lenses and contact the eye doctor right away?
choices: Mild lens awareness in the first week, even without redness or pain
Only a complete loss of vision in one eye
Only redness lasting more than a week, since mild redness is normal at first
Unusual redness, pain, blurred vision, light sensitivity or discharge
explanation: FDA lists discomfort, excess tearing or discharge, unusual light sensitivity, itching, burning or gritty feelings, unusual redness, blurred vision, swelling and pain as symptoms of irritation or infection. Patients should remove lenses and call promptly rather than waiting for severe vision loss.

source.title: FDA: Contact Lens Risks

topic: Case: Itching, mucus and riding lenses
stem: A soft lens wearer reports itching after lens removal, mucus at the inner corner, and lenses that ride up and move too much. Lid eversion shows large papillae on the upper tarsal plate. What is the most likely condition and management?
choices: CLARE: antibiotic drops while continuing wear
Tight lens: flatten the base curve
GPC: stop wear, refer, and consider daily disposables
Dry eye: add rewetting drops only
explanation: Contact Lens Spectrum lists itching after removal, mucus, increased lens movement and large papillae on the palpebral conjunctiva as hallmarks of contact lens papillary conjunctivitis. Management includes discontinuing wear, shorter replacement schedules or daily disposables, addressing deposits, and medications from the doctor.

source.title: Contact Lens Spectrum: Treatment Plan (CLPC/GPC), January 2005

stem: To check a contact lens wearer for suspected GPC, which examination technique is used?
choices: Evert the upper lid; use fluorescein to highlight papillae
A push-up test to see whether the lens moves too freely
Over-keratometry to see whether the lens surface is distorting
Retinoscopy through the lens to check for lid-induced blur
explanation: GPC affects the palpebral (tarsal) conjunctiva, which is seen only by everting the upper lid at the slit lamp. Contact Lens Spectrum notes sodium fluorescein readily highlights the large to giant "white-capped" papillae. The other tests assess lens fit, not the lids.

source.title: Contact Lens Spectrum: Treatment Plan (CLPC/GPC), January 2005

stem: A soft lens wearer using a multipurpose solution reports burning shortly after inserting lenses straight from the case, and both eyes are mildly red. What is the most likely cause and approach?
choices: Inverted lenses; teach the taco test and reinsert both
Solution sensitivity; stop wear until seen, then a peroxide system may help
CLPU; continue wear and monitor for 24-48 hours
Tight lens syndrome from lens dehydration in the case; flatten the base curve
explanation: Contact Lens Spectrum links burning shortly after application, and some red eyes with infiltrates, to sensitivity to the multipurpose solution; switching to a preservative-free hydrogen peroxide system resolved the case it describes. A red, uncomfortable eye still warrants removing the lenses and having the doctor evaluate it.

source.title: Contact Lens Spectrum: Practical Red Eye Problem-Solving

stem: A patient rinsed his lenses with his roommate's red-capped hydrogen peroxide solution right before insertion, and his eyes burned badly. What happened?
choices: Unneutralized peroxide reached the eye
An allergy to the lens material triggered by the solution
The lenses were inserted inside out
A normal reaction to peroxide that fades with use
