explanation: FDA warns never to rinse lenses with non-neutralized hydrogen peroxide or put it directly in the eye; it can cause stinging, burning, irritation or eye damage. The red tip and cap flag peroxide products. Lenses must soak in the supplied case for the labeled time so neutralization is complete.

source.title: FDA: Hydrogen Peroxide Solution

stem: A peroxide-system user opened a new bottle but kept using her old lens case, and now her lenses sting on insertion. Why?
choices: The new bottle was contaminated with tap water at the factory
Peroxide doesn't need neutralizing, so the stinging must be an allergy to it
Her lenses are inside out after soaking in the new solution
The old case may no longer neutralize; use each bottle's new case
explanation: FDA's safety tips: always use the new case that comes with every bottle; an old case will not neutralize the peroxide and may cause stinging, burning, irritation or eye damage when lenses go back on the eye.

source.title: FDA: Hydrogen Peroxide Solution

stem: A patient says she saves money by adding fresh solution on top of what's already in her lens case. What is the best response?
choices: Topping off is fine if it's within a week
Never top off; discard old solution and use fresh every time
Topping off is fine with peroxide systems only
Stretch the solution with a little tap water instead
explanation: FDA says do not top off the solution in the case; discard all leftover solution after each use and never reuse it. CDC similarly says avoid mixing fresh and old solution. Reused solution loses disinfecting power and lets contamination build up.

source.title: FDA: Contact Lens Risks

topic: Case: Rinsing lenses with tap water
stem: A patient rinses her lenses with tap water because "it's treated and safe to drink." What should you teach?
choices: Distilled water is an acceptable, sterile substitute for solution
Tap water isn't sterile and can carry Acanthamoeba; use solution
Tap water is fine if it's run through a household filter first
Tap water is fine for GP lenses, which don't absorb it
explanation: CDC explains that Acanthamoeba is commonly found in tap water and can cause a severe, hard-to-treat keratitis, so lenses and cases should never be rinsed or stored in water. FDA adds that distilled water and homemade saline are also non-sterile and must not be used.

source.title: CDC: Keeping Water Away from Contact Lenses

stem: A wearer accidentally showered with her reusable lenses in. Per CDC guidance, what should she do with them?
choices: Keep wearing them, but remove them before bedtime tonight
Rinse them with tap water and reinsert them right away
Discard them, or clean and disinfect overnight before reuse
Rewet them with saline drops and keep wearing them, since showers are short
explanation: CDC's water guidance says contact lenses and water are a bad combination, even when showering, and that lenses that touch water should be thrown away or cleaned and disinfected overnight before being worn again.

source.title: CDC: Keeping Water Away from Contact Lenses

stem: A competitive swimmer wants to see clearly in the pool. What is the best advice?
choices: Wear daily disposables in the pool; chlorine makes it safe
Swimming in lenses is safe if the eyes stay closed underwater
Rinse the lenses with tap water after each swim
Remove lenses for swimming and consider prescription goggles
explanation: CDC advises removing lenses before swimming or showering and suggests prescription goggles for people active in water sports who need to see. Chlorine does not reliably remove the risk of water-borne organisms such as Acanthamoeba.

source.title: CDC: Keeping Water Away from Contact Lenses

stem: Per CDC guidance, how should a lens case be cared for and how often replaced?
choices: Store it wet with caps on, and replace it every month
Clean it weekly with solution; it never needs replacing
Rinse it with hot tap water, store it wet with caps on, and replace it yearly
Rub-rinse with solution, air-dry upside down, replace every 3 months
explanation: CDC's prevention steps: clean the case with solution by rubbing and rinsing, store it upside down with the caps off after each use, and replace it at least once every three months. Water should never be used on the case.

source.title: CDC: Preventing Eye Infections When Wearing Contacts

stem: A patient admits he naps and sometimes sleeps overnight in his daily-wear silicone hydrogel lenses "since they're breathable." What should you tell him?
choices: Silicone hydrogel lenses make overnight wear risk-free
The extra risk applies only to GP lenses
Only naps longer than an hour carry risk
Sleeping in lenses raises infection risk 6-8×, whatever the material
explanation: CDC's MMWR report notes that sleeping in lenses, whether inadvertent, occasional or prescribed, increases the risk of contact lens-related eye infection six- to eightfold and is a risk factor regardless of lens material or frequency. About one third of wearers report sleeping or napping in lenses.

source.title: CDC MMWR: Corneal Infections Associated with Sleeping in Contact Lenses

stem: A new wearer asks how to tell whether a soft lens is inside out. In the taco test, which result means the lens is inverted?
choices: The edges flare outward
The edges roll in and stick together
The lens folds completely flat
The edges curve inward and nearly meet
explanation: ACUVUE's guidance: gently pinch the lens as if folding a taco; edges that curve smoothly inward mean it's correct, while edges that flare outward mean it's likely inside out. A saucer-like shape with a flared rim on the fingertip is the same sign.

source.title: ACUVUE: How to tell if your contact lenses are inside out

stem: A patient says a fresh lens feels scratchy, moves around and blurs. Under bright light, the "123" laser marking near the edge reads backward. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The lens is inside out
The lens is torn
She is sensitive to the solution
The lens is too tight
explanation: Some manufacturers laser-mark "123" near the edge; if it reads 1-2-3 the lens is correct, and if the numbers are reversed it's inside out. ACUVUE lists discomfort, excess movement and blurred or distorted vision as symptoms of an inverted lens.

source.title: ACUVUE: How to tell if your contact lenses are inside out

stem: A new soft lens wearer struggles to remove her lenses and has been using her fingernails. What technique should you teach?
choices: Use a GP suction plunger on the soft lens
Grip the lens with the fingernails for a firmer hold
Look up, pull the lower lid down, and pinch with the finger pads
Blink hard while pulling the outer corner of the lids
explanation: ACUVUE's pinch method: look up, hold the lids open, and gently pinch the lens with the pads of the thumb and forefinger, not the nails, which risk injuring the eye. The blink-and-pull technique is for rigid lenses and doesn't apply to soft lenses.

source.title: ACUVUE: How to remove your contact lenses

topic: Case: Hazy, bumpy group IV lenses
stem: A wearer of high-water ionic (group IV) monthly lenses has been stretching them to three months. Vision is hazy, and the lenses show an opaque film and small raised whitish bumps. What is the most likely cause and best management?
choices: Protein deposits and calculi; replace on schedule or go daily
Fungal growth; soak the lenses in antibiotic drops
A tight fit; flatten the base curve
Lipid deposits typical of silicone hydrogels; switch to tap-water rinsing
explanation: Review of Cornea & Contact Lenses notes protein deposits form an opaque film and are especially common in high-water ionic group IV materials, and that lens calculi ("jelly bumps") are also more common in those materials. Management includes increasing or reinforcing replacement frequency, rubbing and rinsing, or refitting into daily disposables.

source.title: Review of Cornea & Contact Lenses: The How and Why of Contact Lens Deposits

topic: Case: Comfort fades late in the cycle
stem: A monthly-lens wearer says comfort is fine for about three weeks and then drops off. What is the most likely cause and fix?
choices: Overwear hypoxia; extend wearing time
Late-cycle deposits; replace more often or use daily disposables
Solution sensitivity; stop rubbing the lenses so less solution is used
A tight lens that has dehydrated over the month; flatten the base curve
explanation: Contact Lens Spectrum ties discomfort near the end of the replacement cycle to surface deposits and suggests reviewing rubbing and replacement compliance, replacing monthly lenses more often (for example, every three weeks), or switching to daily disposables.

source.title: Contact Lens Spectrum: Stop the Cycle (contact lens dropout), Nov-Dec 2026

stem: A soft lens wearer is comfortable in the morning but has dryness and discomfort late in the day, worse after long computer sessions. Which management direction does the guidance emphasize?
choices: Begin sleeping in the lenses so the eyes adapt to them
Increase daily wearing time gradually to build tolerance to dryness
Tear film and MGD care: lid hygiene, warm compresses, full blinks
Steepen the base curve to reduce lens movement late in the day
explanation: Contact Lens Spectrum associates end-of-day discomfort with tear-film instability and meibomian gland dysfunction. It recommends lid hygiene, warm compresses and massage, reminders to blink fully during device use, and options like daily disposables or a peroxide care system.

source.title: Contact Lens Spectrum: Stop the Cycle (contact lens dropout), Nov-Dec 2026

topic: Case: Sudden discomfort with a new lens
stem: A long-time wearer suddenly has discomfort right after inserting a new lens from the same box she's always used. What is the first step?
choices: Switch to a larger diameter so the edge sits under the lids
Remove and inspect the lens for a tear, defect or deposit
Extend wearing time so the lens can settle onto the eye
Keep wearing it; a new lens from the box always needs a day
explanation: Contact Lens Spectrum advises that discomfort of recent onset immediately after application should prompt inspection of the lens surface for deposits and the edge for tears; consistent symptoms point instead to solution sensitivity, contamination or damage. Never keep wearing a lens that hurts.

source.title: Contact Lens Spectrum: Stop the Cycle (contact lens dropout), Nov-Dec 2026

stem: A high myope wearing low-Dk hydrogel lenses 16 hours a day shows limbal redness, new vessels growing into the peripheral cornea and microcysts, and her myopia has steadily increased. What is the most likely cause and management?
choices: Chronic hypoxia; refer and refit a higher-Dk lens, less wear
A loose fit; steepen the base curve
Normal age-related change; no action
Seasonal allergy; antihistamines while continuing wear
explanation: Contact Lens Spectrum lists limbal hyperemia, corneal neovascularization, microcysts and myopic creep as signs of hypoxia from long hours in low-oxygen-transmitting lenses, especially in thicker, higher-power lenses. Higher-Dk materials (such as silicone hydrogel), shorter wear and doctor follow-up address it.

source.title: Contact Lens Spectrum: Practical Red Eye Problem-Solving

stem: A soft lens wearer has itching in both eyes, most intense at the inner corners, with white stringy discharge every spring. What is the most likely condition and approach?
choices: Peroxide toxicity; switch to tap-water rinsing
Ocular allergy; refer for anti-allergy drops, reduce wear
Microbial keratitis; patch the eye
CLARE; antibiotics and overnight wear
explanation: Contact Lens Spectrum describes ocular allergy as bilateral injection with itching (often most intense nasally) and white stringy discharge, from allergens collecting in the tear film. Management includes lid hygiene and antihistamine/mast-cell stabilizer drops, which the eye doctor prescribes.

source.title: Contact Lens Spectrum: Practical Red Eye Problem-Solving

topic: Case: Releasing a contact lens Rx
stem: After a soft lens fitting is completed, the office says it will release the prescription only if the patient buys lenses there or signs a liability waiver. Is this allowed under the FTC Contact Lens Rule?
choices: Yes, a reasonable release fee can be charged in place of a lens purchase
No; it must be released after the fitting, with no purchase or waiver
Only if the patient requests the prescription in writing
Yes, as long as the waiver is in writing and kept on file
explanation: The FTC guide says prescribers must provide the prescription immediately at the end of a contact lens fitting, even if the patient doesn't ask, and cannot require patients to buy lenses, pay additional fees or sign a waiver or release in exchange for it.

source.title: FTC: The Contact Lens Rule - A Guide for Prescribers and Sellers

stem: An online seller sends a complete verification request, and the prescriber doesn't respond within 8 business hours. What happens under the FTC rule?
choices: The seller must cancel the order
It is treated as verified, and the seller may ship
The seller must wait 40 more business hours
The seller may substitute a different brand
explanation: Under the FTC Contact Lens Rule, the prescriber has 8 business hours to respond to a complete verification request; if there's no response, the prescription is passively verified and the seller may provide the lenses. (40 business hours applies to providing a copy of the Rx to a patient's designated agent.)

source.title: FTC: The Contact Lens Rule - A Guide for Prescribers and Sellers

stem: A prescriber wants routine contact lens prescriptions to expire after 6 months. What does the FTC rule allow?
choices: At least one year, unless a documented medical reason applies
A two-year minimum for all soft and GP lenses
Six months, which is the federal standard
Any expiration the prescriber chooses, with or without a reason
explanation: The FTC rule sets a floor of one year for contact lens prescription expiration unless there is a legitimate medical reason, which must be documented and kept for at least three years. A state law requiring a longer period governs for prescribers in that state.

source.title: FTC: The Contact Lens Rule - A Guide for Prescribers and Sellers

topic: Case: Brand substitution by a seller
stem: A seller wants to substitute a cheaper brand for the lens that was prescribed. What does the FTC rule allow?
choices: Any brand with matching base curve, diameter and power, since the fit is identical
Any brand made of a similar silicone hydrogel material
Only an identical private-label lens from the same manufacturer
Any brand, as long as the patient agrees to the switch
explanation: Sellers may not alter a prescription. The FTC guide's only exception is substituting identical lenses made by the same manufacturer and sold under a different name (private label). Matching base curve and diameter is not equivalence, because material and design affect fit and safety.

source.title: FTC: The Contact Lens Rule - A Guide for Prescribers and Sellers

stem: A patient's spectacle Rx is -6.00 DS at a 12 mm vertex distance. What soft lens power, rounded to the nearest 0.25 D, corrects at the corneal plane?
explanation: Effective power at the cornea is F / (1 - dF) = -6.00 / (1 + 0.012 × 6.00) = -6.00 / 1.072 ≈ -5.60 D, which rounds to -5.50 D. Minus lenses need less power at the cornea than at the spectacle plane; CooperVision's guide likewise starts from the vertex-corrected spherical equivalent.

source.title: CooperVision: Multifocal Contact Lens Fitting Guides

stem: A patient's refraction is -2.00 -0.50 × 180, and you're choosing a spherical soft multifocal trial lens. Per GPLI's pocket guide, what starting distance power should you use?
choices: -2.50 D, the sphere plus full cylinder
-1.75 D, the sphere minus half the cylinder
-2.00 D, the sphere power alone
-2.25 D, the spherical equivalent
explanation: GPLI recommends that the initial soft multifocal power equal the spherical equivalent of the manifest refraction at the corneal plane: sphere + half the cylinder = -2.00 + (-0.25) = -2.25 D. At this power, the vertex effect is negligible. Final powers should favor least minus, most plus.

source.title: GPLI: Contact Lens Clinical Pearls Pocket Guide

stem: A patient on a tight budget asks whether homemade saline or distilled water can be used to rinse and store his lenses. What is the best answer?
choices: No; use only fresh, sterile commercial solution
Yes, because distilled water is sterile
Yes, but for rinsing only
Yes, if the saline is boiled first
explanation: FDA says never to use non-sterile water (distilled water, tap water or any homemade saline) with contact lenses and to avoid exposing lenses to any water. Non-sterile liquids can introduce organisms, including Acanthamoeba, that cause serious keratitis.

source.title: FDA: Contact Lens Risks
